limitations: One engine-assisted reviewer used the original Stockfish candidate and played-move comparison lines. Labels were frozen before the candidate or any comparison output was inspected. Uncertain judgments are explicit.

cases.rationale: Qg3+ and Bd4+ gain tempi against the exposed king. Qxd4 inverts the checking order and gives up the queen, while Ng3 lets the king out.
Rh8+ forces king movement before the knight gives check and both rooks are exchanged on d8. A slower rook move misses that concrete liquidation.
The Nf7+ and Nd6+ checks can repeat to hold the ending. Ng8 lets Black give checks and take h5. The precise contribution of the fixed pawns as a strategic feature is unclear.
Rg5+ starts a forcing rook attack with Rf3+ and Rf2+. The quieter b6 and Re3 lines instead contain the d-pawn and reposition the rooks.
Black can use the open d-file or double on the c-file. White's rook activity and the c-pawn are common concerns in the near-equal lines.
The choice between doubling on the f-file, contesting the c-file and playing h4 changes which files each side can use. The small score differences reflect similar positions.
Rf1 sets up Rf4 and a central d-pawn advance while dxe4 and Qf2 allow distinct queen exchanges or captures with check. Control of the f- and e-files persists.
The rook can swing to f3 or contest the d-file. The alternatives allow different exchanges on e3 and d4, including a concrete path for the d-pawn.
Re5 brings a rook into play before Bxf5 and the captures on e6. The bishop retreat or check changes which pawns can advance and whether the rook can use that file.
Re8 holds the defence before the bishop takes c5. Rd8 or Rc6 permits Bb7 and Bxa8 during the rook recapture, with a distinct cost to Black's rook coordination.
Re8 supports Rxe4 after the knight trade. The alternate rook squares give White a different response and change Black's use of the e-file and counterplay around the king.
Rb1 gains a queen tempo and realigns both rooks. After Be7 Black can trade on c5 and d8, changing the pressure from the queenside pawns.
White can choose a bishop exchange or place the rook on b1. The critical play involves the a-pawn and the rook's access to the c-file. Several short exchanges lack a common forcing payoff.
Both players choose between placing a rook on the d-file and keeping pawn moves available. Black's bishop and queenside pawn decisions vary across near-equal lines.
Qb3 changes the queen trade and enables Bxb2 after the rooks take d1. The rook alternative uses d3 to support advancing queenside pawns instead.
Rhe8 and Nd5 change the entry Qxc4+ and whether there is a knight capture on c3. Control of the e-file and White's e-pawn remain central.
Ng6+ deflects the f-pawn before Qh8+ and Rh7+. The other rook routes change the forcing king attack rather than achieving the same result.
Nxa2+ gains a tempo and changes the sequence in which White can take c4. The alternative king and knight placements leave Black short of counterplay against the c-pawn and bishops.
The rook can capture the e-pawn with check or take it after moving the bishop. The king and rook routes determine how to blockade Black's a-pawn.
Black tries to coordinate the queen and king while reorganizing the kingside pawns. The played check changes White's king square without resolving the strategic disadvantage.
Pushing g3 changes the queen's checking entry and promotion threat. Qh6 retains both f- and g-pawns while the other queen check allows a different queen trade.
The alternatives can trade rooks before or after queen repositioning. The resulting queen activity and choice of pawn targets persist without a demonstrated narrow tactical requirement.
The choice between resolving cxd4 and checking changes how White can use the f-file. The leading positions differ mainly in the central pawn structure and rook activity.
Qe3+ is the route to perpetual check. The rook and king alternatives let White use a concerted attack and materially different captures.
The checks and lateral rook moves influence which rook reaches the seventh. The candidates leave different exchanges and give different routes to the passed pawns.
The king and bishop choices address different knight routes. The core question concerns containing the a- and h-pawns with a bishop against the knight.
Rd8+ forces a perpetual via Qxd8+ and Qc7+. The quieter alternatives need a separate concrete route against Black's threats.
Rg7+ gives White time to take g6 and e6 while the knight checks and captures. The quieter method of repeating with Nf6+ leaves the central pawns where they are.
c5 and c6 allow the same dxc6 reply through different capture rules, while cxb3 allows a forcing rook exchange on a7. The resulting central and queenside files govern plans.
The queen trade, rook manoeuvres and e-pawn restriction define the choices. The observed tactical exchanges leave the same broad material disadvantage.
Black uses the active king and queenside majority in several move orders. The conversion concerns pawn breaks and opposition.
The rook from g8 must give check so that the a-rook remains to limit the checked king. The alternatives give White a decisive queen check and counterattack.
cxd4 removes the knight without giving up Black's rook for it. a6 allows Nf5+ and a forcing exchange. The c- and d-files organise the counterplay.
White's rooks can force exchanges on e8 or mate after g6. Black's available knight moves alter the forcing continuation.
h5 keeps the kingside pressure and permits the Rxe5 sequence before Qxf2+. The bishop alternatives give Black different e- and d-pawn moves.
Ngf8 and axb4 can occur in either order and change who recaptures on c5. Nh4 makes the kingside exchanges concrete and gives up queenside control.
The queen maneuvers against the bishop and moves the king before the f-pawn lever. The choice of queen square changes the long-term role of the central pawn.
Bxg5 changes the kingside pawn structure. The other choices allow the rook exchange on e3 or Bxf4, while Black's advancing c-pawn continues to shape the position.
The bishop and king support different penetration routes before the h-pawn is taken. The root moves all convert the same endgame advantage.
gxf4 permits the knight fork after Kxf7, taking the rook on a8. Nxf4+ and Kg1 change the concrete exchange sequence.
Each rook move retains king and pawn coordination, and keeps the option of advancing e4. White's exchange sacrifice in one line does not establish a required tactic at the root.
Qg3+ is followed by Bxf2 and a queen entry, while the captures on f5 resolve the central attacker differently. The e-pawn and king shelter remain strategic concerns.
Rxg5 exchanges rooks before Bxg5. The alternative bishop captures preserve more pieces and change king and knight placement around the d-pawn.
Nxe2+ gains the required tempo before Rxe4. Nxf1 and the first rook capture change the recapture sequence decisively.
Rxc4 removes the bishop without surrendering the same f-file activity. bxc4 opens a different file and lets the knight attack the king.
Kf2 changes the checks aimed at White's king, while a3 allows Bxc3+ and the later queen trade. The h-pawn and e-file route change across the alternatives.
White's bishop retreats and flank pawn break all react to c4 and b5. The isolated tactic at the end of one branch does not establish the reason for the original choice.
Qe5 controls the timing of Qxc7 and the rook exchange. Qd6 gives a different liquidation and lets the rook capture on the second rank.
Rg4+ gives a concrete route for the rook on d8 to check the exposed king. Rg2 and Rg6 give White more freedom to move rooks and support the passed e-pawn.
hxg3 removes the advanced threat before the queen enters. Knight moves permit gxh2+ and a materially different exchange, while the kingside files and cover persist.
Different captures on d5 change the forcing e4 and Nb5 sequences. The underlying c-, d- and f-pawn structure affects the chosen rook and knight plans.
Black can place the rook on c3 or d3 before pressuring the bishop and queenside pawn. The h-pawn choice keeps a distinct structure with close evaluations.
The bishop and rook manoeuvres choose how to meet the d-pawn break and White's h-file access. The variations do not settle on a specific tactical requirement at the root.
Bh2+ can force a repetition, while Be5 and Kh8 use the knight entry on d3. White's queenside pawn majority changes what the rook trades achieve.
The timing of fxg4 or Kh8 changes the captures and rook entry against the king. The locked queenside pawns and opening g-file explain why the attack stays on one wing.
